awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I:  High-throughput platform for small molecule, in-cell targeting of undruggable proteins via their mRNAs
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will be improvement of the health and welfare of Americans by providing an efficient and cost-effective approach for developing therapeutics for previously undruggable diseases, including hard to treat neurodegenerative diseases and highly aggressive cancers. Most diseases are targeted at the protein level using small molecule drugs, but only 600 proteins have ever been drugged directly.  This collective human effort has left the majority of roughly 3,000 disease-related genes in humans undrugged and unable to be drugged using conventional pharmaceutical technology. Messenger RNAs (mRNAs) lie upstream of protein expression and, in principle, can be targeted to modulate protein function and treat disease. However, the physical and chemical properties of mRNAs present unique challenges not faced during protein-based drug discovery, and there has been little success in targeting mRNAs using small molecules. This project will address this unmet need by developing small molecule drugs against hard to treat and previously undruggable diseases by targeting their mRNAs directly. 

The proposed project will enable critical technical innovations needed to ensure the technical and commercial viability of a nascent drug discovery platform making it high-throughput and cost effective. The high throughput drug discovery platform to be developed creates an efficient path to screen for high-value drug assets and creates multiple pathways to new classes of therapeutics. The drug discovery platform currently has outstanding robustness and accuracy in defining interactions between small molecules and mRNAs in cells. However, the platform includes bespoke and hands-on steps and will remain a research-lab-only tool without critical innovations. The proposed project will improve the platform to be capable of fully automated ligand screening in cells using a library of complex small molecules optimized to bind mRNA. Methods will be developed to screen multiplexed samples, in a quantitative way. Automation will require the integration of diverse, novel methodologies, and data deconvolution.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Project Outcomes Report

ForagR Medicines is developing a novel drug discovery platform capable of targeting previously undruggable disease-associated mRNAs with small molecules. The ForagR platform is the first of its kind to allow for identification of mRNA-ligand binding sites and function-modulating small molecules, transcriptome wide, without requiring a priori structural knowledge of targets. The platform leverages fragment-based drug discovery principles where compounds, or "high-complexity fragments" used for screening are chosen at the earliest stages to have optimal chemical properties including high-complexity interactions with mRNA, membrane permeability, and minimal toxicity to live cells. The platform simultaneously yields: (i) high-quality chemical matter, (ii) highly specific hits transcriptome-wide, (iii) assessments across broad classes of mRNA targets and disease states, (iv) selectivity against abundant and non-target RNAs, and (v) target sites with complex, ligandable RNA structures. The ForagR platform thus solves multiple challenges in RNA-targeted medicines and arrives at lead assets and function efficiently.

The overarching goals for Phase I were to accelerate critical technical innovations needed to ensure the technical and commercial viability of the ForagR platform. We successfully completed all Phase I milestones. First, we successfully achieved our Phase I milestone of developing and validating an automated, high-throughput screening platform capable of identifying RNA-binding fragments against clinically relevant and previously undruggable targets. Second, we identified a potent lead molecule that bound the mRNA of a well-validated but undruggable protein target implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple forms of cancer, including hepatocellular carcinoma and colorectal cancer.

Our lead molecule was selected for further optimization and progression studies in Phase II, based on its cellular activity and target selectivity and its ability to demonstrate the overall power of our drug discovery platform. The identification of this promising lead provides a clear development candidate and significantly reduces technical risk associated with advancing RNA-targeted therapeutics toward preclinical evaluation and commercialization.

This successful Phase I project marks the transition of the ForagR platform from a research tool to a validated, high-throughput, cost effective engine for RNA therapeutics discovery. This project further validates the NSF SBIR/STTR program mandate of funding development of high-risk technology innovations intended to generate positive societal outcomes. The ForagR platform will significantly improve the health and welfare of Americans by proving an efficient and cost-effective way to develop therapeutics for previously undruggable diseases, including cancers and neurodegenerative diseases. High-value targets for both disease groups are commonly either conventionally undruggable by virtue of not having ligandable pockets or being intrinsically disordered and are prime candidates to be targeted at the RNA level using fragments optimized to penetrate solid tissues and blood brain barrier. Given the effectiveness of the ForagR platform, the company is well positioned to capture a significant portion of the $5B-plus RNA-targeting small molecule market.
